## Topics covered

-   The multiple linear regression model
-   Interpreting the coefficients, at fixed values of the other variables
-   Tests, confidence intervals and predictions with several explanatory
    variables
-   A qualitative explanatory variable

::: callout-note
#### Note

The exercises associated with this unit are available at
[this link](https://tommasorigon.github.io/EnvEcoStat/exe/exe_D.html).
:::

## Back to the black cherry trees

In [Unit K](un_K.html) we predicted the volume of timber of $n = 31$ black
cherry trees from the [diameter]{.blue} of their trunk. The unit ended with an
observation: the volume does not depend on the diameter only, since taller
trees have, on average, more timber.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Does the [height]{.orange} of a tree help to predict its volume, once the
diameter is known?
:::

We build the same data frame of [Unit K](un_K.html):

```{r}
cherry <- data.frame(
  diameter = round(trees$Girth * 2.54, 1), # cm
  height = round(trees$Height * 0.3048, 1), # m
  volume = round(trees$Volume * 0.0283168, 3) # cubic metres
)
summary(cherry)
```

## Scatterplot matrix

With three variables, the command `pairs` draws all the scatterplots at once,
and `cor` applied to the data frame returns all the correlations:

```{r}
pairs(cherry, pch = 16)
round(cor(cherry), 2)
```

The volume is strongly related to the diameter and, less strongly, to the
height. Note also that the two explanatory variables are [related to each
other]{.orange}: taller trees tend to have a larger diameter.

## The multiple linear regression model

The [multiple linear regression model]{.orange} with two explanatory variables
assumes that $$
Y_i = \alpha + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i, \qquad i = 1,\dots,n,
$$ where $x_{i1}$ is the diameter and $x_{i2}$ the height of the $i$th tree.
As in [Unit K](un_K.html), the values $x_{i1}$ and $x_{i2}$ are treated as
fixed, and the errors $\epsilon_1,\dots,\epsilon_n$ are independent, with
distribution $\text{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. Therefore:

-   $\alpha + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2$ is the [mean]{.blue} volume of the
    trees with diameter $x_1$ and height $x_2$;
-   $\beta_1$ is the change in the mean volume when the diameter increases by
    $1$ cm, [at fixed height]{.orange};
-   $\beta_2$ is the change in the mean volume when the height increases by
    $1$ m, [at fixed diameter]{.orange}.

The estimates $\hat{\alpha}$, $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_2$ are again
obtained by [least squares]{.blue}, that is by minimising $$
\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \alpha - \beta_1 x_{i1} - \beta_2 x_{i2})^2.
$$ There is no simple formula as in [Unit F](un_F.html): we let **R** do the
computations.

## The command `lm`

The explanatory variables are listed in the formula, separated by `+`:

```{r}
fit <- lm(volume ~ diameter + height, data = cherry)
coef(fit)
```

For two trees with the [same height]{.blue}, one additional centimetre of
diameter corresponds, on average, to $0.053$ m$^3$ of additional timber. For
two trees with the [same diameter]{.blue}, one additional metre of height
corresponds, on average, to $0.031$ m$^3$ of additional timber. In short, we
say that these are the effects of the diameter and of the height, each
[adjusting for]{.orange} the other variable.

## The command `summary`

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

The output is read as in [Unit K](un_K.html), with a few differences:

-   in the table `Coefficients`, each row tests $H_0: \beta_j = 0$, that is,
    whether the variable is useful [given the other one]{.blue}. The height has
    a P-value of $0.016$: it helps to predict the volume, even when the
    diameter is known;
-   the variance $\sigma^2$ is estimated by $s^2 = \frac{1}{n - 3}\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2$,
    because three parameters have been estimated: `Residual standard error` is
    $s$, with $n - 3 = 28$ degrees of freedom;
-   the last line is the [F test]{.orange} of $H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = 0$,
    that is, whether [at least one]{.blue} of the variables is useful. Here the
    P-value is practically zero.

The coefficient $R^2$ increases from $0.935$ (diameter only, [Unit
K](un_K.html)) to $0.948$.

## Confidence intervals

As in [Unit K](un_K.html), the $95\%$ confidence intervals are obtained with
`confint`:

```{r}
confint(fit)
```

## Marginal and conditional effects

What if we used the [height only]{.blue}?

```{r}
fit_height <- lm(volume ~ height, data = cherry)
coef(fit_height)
```

Alone, one additional metre of height corresponds to $0.142$ m$^3$ of
additional timber: almost [five times]{.orange} the value $0.031$ obtained at
fixed diameter. Why?

Taller trees also tend to have a larger diameter. The simple regression
attributes to the height also the effect of the diameter, which is not in the
model. The multiple regression, instead, compares trees with the same
diameter.

::: callout-warning
The coefficient of a variable [depends on which other variables]{.orange} are
in the model. Always interpret it together with the list of the other
variables: "at fixed ...".
:::

## Prediction

Two standing trees have the same diameter, $40$ cm, but different heights,
$20$ m and $25$ m. The data frame given to `predict` must now contain both
variables:

```{r}
new_trees <- data.frame(diameter = c(40, 40), height = c(20, 25))
predict(fit, newdata = new_trees, interval = "prediction")
```

The taller tree is expected to have about $0.16$ m$^3$ of additional timber.
As in [Unit K](un_K.html), `interval = "confidence"` would instead give the
intervals for the mean volume.

## Residual plots

```{r}
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit),
  pch = 16,
  xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = "dashed")
```

As in [Unit K](un_K.html), a slight [curvature]{.orange} is still visible: the
model is useful, but it is only an approximation.

## A qualitative explanatory variable

Let us go back to the `Houses` data of [Exercises B](exe/exe_B.html): the
selling price (`price`, thousands of dollars) and the size (`size`, square
feet) of $100$ houses, and whether the house is new (`new`, $1 =$ yes,
$0 =$ no).

```{r}
path <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Houses.dat"
Houses <- read.table(path, header = TRUE)
Houses$new <- factor(Houses$new, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes"))
```

::: callout-note
#### Research question

Are new houses more expensive than old ones? By how much?
:::

A qualitative variable can be included in `lm` as any other variable:

```{r}
fit_new <- lm(price ~ new, data = Houses)
coef(fit_new)
```

**R** creates the [indicator]{.blue} variable `newyes`, equal to $1$ for new
houses and $0$ for old ones. The model is then
$\text{price} = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{newyes}$, so that $\alpha$ is the
mean price of old houses and $\beta$ is the [difference]{.orange} between the
mean prices of new and old houses. The first category, `no`, is the
[reference category]{.blue}: it has no indicator. With $c$ categories, **R**
creates $c - 1$ indicators, one for each category except the first.

```{r}
price_no <- Houses$price[Houses$new == "no"]
price_yes <- Houses$price[Houses$new == "yes"]
mean(price_no)
mean(price_yes) - mean(price_no)
```

## Adjusting for the size

New houses are, however, also [larger]{.orange}:

```{r}
boxplot(size ~ new, data = Houses)
```

Let us compare new and old houses [of the same size]{.blue}:

```{r}
fit_size_new <- lm(price ~ size + new, data = Houses)
summary(fit_size_new)
```

At fixed size, a new house costs on average $87$ thousand dollars more than
an old one, and not $229$: a large part of the difference between the two
groups is due to the size. The difference remains statistically significant
(P-value $0.003$).

This is the same phenomenon seen with the trees: the effect of a variable
changes when another variable, related to both, enters the model. The size is
a [confounding variable]{.orange} for the comparison between new and old
houses.

::: callout-warning
These are [observational]{.blue} data: association does not imply causation.
Adjusting for the size removes its effect, but other variables that are not in
the data (the neighbourhood, the quality of the materials, ...) could still
explain part of the difference.
:::
